Posted January 13, 2003
Analysis by Richard Cowan

As I reported last week, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien had seemed to be throwing cold water on his own Justice Minister's calls for acting on some sort of decriminalization bill early this year.
See
 Canadian Health Minister Seeks Asylum In DEAland; Says Making Her Think About Medical Cannabis Constitutes Torture. In DC They Don't Allow That Sort of Thing. Thinking, That Is.

In a parliamentary system this sort of split makes even less sense than it would in DEAland. However, after yet another Ontario court threw out a possession case saying that the law as it currently stands in Ontario " no longer exists " and is " an offence not known to law, " he had to try to say something coherent. Sort of

In a truly bizarre move, in order to prove that he is prepared to move quickly, the PM's office released transcripts of a justice committee hearing in 1980, in which Chrétien, then the Justice Minister, is quoted as supporting decriminalization of small amounts, so that young people " will not have a stigma for the rest of their lives. "

This man has been Prime Minister since November 4, 1993, with an absolute lock on Parliament, and is scheduled to retire early next year! Hundreds of thousands of young Canadians have gotten a stigma for the rest of their lives " on his watch!

This reminds me of Bill Clinton's saying that marijuana should be decriminalized as he was leaving office. Somehow the word loathsome comes to mind.
See
 Clinton Says Marijuana Should Be Decriminalized. Now He Tells Us!

The problem is that changing the personal possession laws will not address the point being raised by the Ontario courts. The reason that possession is " an offence not known to law " in Canada's largest province is that the federal government has failed to provide a realistic way of taking care of the needs of patients who use cannabis.

In effect, the Ontario courts are holding the possession laws hostage to force the government to meet its obligations under a 2000 ruling that the crown did not appeal. However, the latest ruling on Thursday went even further.

Ontario Superior Court Justice Sydney Lederman declared the current Marijuana Medicinal Access Regulations unconstitutional and gave the government until July 9th to come up with a workable program, or the government will have to provide the patients with cannabis.

Lederman's opinion said, " The government must be granted time to fix the MMAR or otherwise provide for a legal source and supply of the drug the MMAR authorize seriously ill individuals to possess and produce, consistent with their security rights.

Access is compromised because there is simply no legal way for individuals with production licences to obtain the marijuana seeds required to grow it. Even if it were somehow acceptable for individuals to rely on black market supplies to exercise their constitutional rights, the unreliability of this source cannot be ignored. "

He added that Consorting with criminal drug dealers strikes me as a relatively risky means of obtaining medicine.

The government has 30 days to decide whether or not to appeal. It did not appeal the 2000 ruling, and got way with delaying things for another year and a half after the deadline, so they may try the same thing again. Either way, sooner rather than later, the Canadian government is going to have to allow the supplying of medical cannabis to patients.

They simply do not have a clue as to how to put the square peg of herbal cannabis into the round hole designed for pharmaceuticals in the context of cannabis prohibition.

If it were not for prohibition, it would be very easy to recognize that cannabis belongs under the herbal medicine category, which is more advanced in Canada than in DEAland. They may have to use that loophole, but it will just be a cover for de facto legalization, because cannabis has so many uses and is so much safer than even most legal herbs.

Inasmuch as the ideological needs of the prohibitionists always come before the medical needs of the patients, such a common sense approach will be difficult.

But then there is the Canadian Supreme Court. They are not likely to be amused by this latest bit of double-talk from the PM.

In December, they delayed hearing the constitutional challenges until this Spring, because the Canadian Attorney General was saying one thing in public and another thing in Court.
See
 Canadian Supreme Court Punts On Cannabis Cases Until Spring. The Games Governments Play Prove The Need for International Debate on Cannabis Prohibition. Special to MarijuanaNews

The PM has now been on both sides, so it is not unreasonable to hope that the Supreme Court Justices will be even more irritated by this latest maneuver, and there is a very good chance that they will throw out the possession laws, and perhaps even the sales prohibitions, late in the year.

The worse the decrim law that the Parliament passes turns out to be, the more likely they are to rule that it violates the Charter of Rights, which says, " The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. "

It seems impossible, given the lower court rulings, that the prohibition of medical cannabis will survive such a challenge. The questions of fact are all on our side.

It has been widely suggested, even by people close to the PM, that he may prefer to have the Courts take care of the whole mess. That gets him off the hook domestically, and, perhaps even more importantly, with DEAland. He can always tell John Walters that they would love to put kids and jail and deprive the sick and dying of medicine, but gosh and golly, the courts just want let them.
See
 As Canada Moves Toward Some Form Of Decriminalization, Canadian Narks and Walters Escalate Lying. The New Math. Canada Replaces Mexico As Leading Supplier of Cannabis. And If You Believe That
and links

In the meantime, only the compassion clubs are providing for the patients, and the recalcitrance of the medical establishment, a.k.a. organized quackery, means that distribution will almost have to be outside of the pharmaceutical system, and left to the cannabis community.

As a comic backdrop to this, Gordon Campbell, the prohibitionist Premier of British Columbia was arrested on a DUI charge in Maui this weekend, and his mug shots were on the front page of every paper in Canada. His provincial Attorney General is a party-line prohibitionist, who opposes cannabis decrim with really retrograde reefer madness. In short, it couldn't happen to a more deserving fellow.

In the last year, the Premier of neighboring Alberta has admitted to having a drinking problem, as has the Canadian Defense Minister. Campbell is joining a distinguished group on the water wagon. Today the papers are reporting that head of one of the largest native groups in Canada was suspended over an alcohol related assault.

But the prohibitionists say that allowing sick people to use cannabis would send the wrong message to children that cannabis is harmless like alcohol and other things that are legal for adults, like being the Premier of BC.
